thesis: Ismail al-Jazari's 1206 Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices described 50 machines, including a boat of mechanical musicians run by pegs on a turning drum. Storing a sequence in physical form for a machine to follow leads indirectly to robots that learn.

story.title: A band that plays itself
story.text: In his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, written for the Artuqid court in Diyarbakır, al-Jazari described a boat of four mechanical musicians for royal parties. Water power turned a drum. Pegs on the drum pushed levers, and the levers made the drummers strike. He gave building instructions so others could make it.

story.title: Move the pegs, change the tune
story.text: Each peg lifts a lever as the drum turns past it, and when the peg moves on, the drummer's arm falls and strikes. The pegs are a stored sequence of instructions. Moved to new holes, they make the same machine play a different rhythm, just as a modern drum machine follows a grid of steps.

story.title: From pegs to policies
story.text: Roboticist Noel Sharkey argues this was an early programmable automaton. The link to AI is long and indirect, but the idea holds: a stored sequence that a machine carries out. Robots once ran fixed code; now many learn their movements from data, as a neural network policy.

hint: Click cells in the unrolled grid to add or remove pegs, then watch the same pegs come round on the drum and the drummers play your new rhythm.
